origin.fact: It is an albino colour form of the oscar, Astronotus ocellatus, a cichlid from the Amazon basin in South America.
Albinos came from captive breeding. One source says the first ones showed up in the 1970s and 1980s and then became a regular trade fish. No named breeder or country is given.
Aquarium breeders have made albino, leucistic, xanthistic and stronger-red forms of the oscar.
The albino red tiger is sold as a line bred in captivity from the red tiger oscar. It does not come from a wild population.

looks.fact: A true albino has a near-white body with pink to orange-red markings and pinkish-red eyes.
Clear, bright red eyes are the main sign of a true albino. Dark or dull eyes point to a lutino or mixed genetics.
Albino red tiger: pale cream to peach body with orange-red to coppery-red marbling, and red or pink eyes.
Albinism here is a simple recessive trait: a fish needs two copies of the gene to show it.

lines.fact: Albino tiger: white or cream base with uneven orange-red stripes or patches. This is the most common line.
Albino red: red-orange covers most of the body with little white. Red coverage depends on many genes, so top-quality fish are harder to breed.
Albino ruby: deeper red on the sides and back, with a white belly and face. 'Ruby' is partly a sales label.
Albino lemon: warm yellow body with faint or no stripes. Ruby eyes suggest a true albino, dark eyes a lutino.
Lutino: golden-yellow body with dark red to brown eyes. It is caused by a different recessive gene from albino.
Long-finned oscar varieties have also been bred in recent years.

keeping.fact: Minimum about 208 L for one fish with extra filtration; 284 L is better. More than two fish quickly overcrowd a tank.
A Vietnamese guide gives at least 280 L for one fish, 400–500 L as ideal, and 800 L or more for a pair.
Use a canister filter rated 1.5–2 times the tank volume and change 25–30% of the water each week. Keep ammonia and nitrite at zero.
Albinos are sensitive to light, so use moderate, indirect lighting and floating plants for shade.
Soft sand suits their digging. Fix wood and decor firmly in place, and keep lighting dim.
Staple food is cichlid pellets. Add carotenoid-rich foods such as krill, shrimp and spirulina to keep the red and orange colour. Avoid feeder goldfish.
It eats any fish that fits in its mouth. A species-only tank is best. Severums, arowanas, Jack Dempseys and plecos may work in a big tank.
Do not keep it with small or long-finned fish such as neons, bettas or guppies.
Use a lid, because oscars can jump out.

breeding.fact: Two albinos produce only albino young, so the line breeds true.
Two normal-looking carriers give on average about 25% albino young. Carriers cannot be spotted by looks.
Crossing an albino with a lutino gives wild-coloured young, because the two traits come from different genes.
Pairs clean a flat surface to lay on. Small females lay about 300–500 eggs, large ones 2,500–3,000. Both parents guard the brood.
Oscars mature at about one year and can breed for 9–10 years.
Forced pairings often fail. Fry live on their yolk for 3–4 days, then eat baby brine shrimp.
One guide calls breeding hard in aquariums: sexes are hard to tell apart, mates may fight, and parents may eat eggs or fry.

health.fact: With no melanin, even in the eyes, albinos are sensitive to bright light. They may hide, refuse food or lose colour; dimming the light usually helps within 24–48 hours.
Ich spots and fin damage show up more clearly on pale skin.
Hole-in-the-head disease is linked to poor water, vitamin shortage and feeder fish.
One source says albinos are not less healthy than normally coloured oscars.
Common problems listed: ich, fungus, bacterial ulcers and worms. Prevent them with stable water, clean food and quarantine.

buying.fact: Pick a fish with clear red eyes, a full but not bloated body, smooth skin and open fins, that reacts to you. Avoid fish hiding or hovering listlessly.
Check the shop tank: cloudy water, dead fish or overcrowding raise the risk of hidden disease. Quarantine new fish for at least 2 weeks.
Ask about the parents. Fish sold as 'albino' are often lutino or lemon fish.
Many white oscars sold as albino are actually lutino. These may later develop orange mottling or grey fins.

Watch Vietnamese names: one Vietnamese page sells an 'albino tai tượng' under the peacock bass name Cichla ocellaris with a size of 8–12 cm, so it is not this oscar. 'Tai tượng' is also used for other fish.

controversy.fact: Wikipedia notes that oscars are sometimes artificially coloured ('painted').
Wild oscars released through the aquarium trade have formed feral populations in China, northern Australia and Florida.
Hobbyist writers criticise shops for calling any white oscar 'albino' when many are lutino.
